title: The multiplication principle
instructions: Type each answer and press Check. Steps in a row multiply; fill the most restricted spot first. Stuck? Open a hint.

problems.prompt: You have $[[a]]$ shirts, $[[b]]$ pairs of trousers and $[[c]]$ hats. An outfit is one of each. How many outfits are there?

mistakes.why: You wear a shirt AND trousers AND a hat: multiply, don't add.

hints: Each shirt goes with every pair of trousers and every hat.

problems.prompt: A lock code is $[[k]]$ digits long, and each digit is one of $1, 2, \ldots, [[m]]$. Digits may repeat. How many codes are possible?

mistakes.why: Each of the $[[k]]$ spots has $[[m]]$ choices: multiply $[[m]]$ by itself $[[k]]$ times, don't multiply $[[m]]$ by $[[k]]$.

hints: Each digit can be chosen in $[[m]]$ ways, whatever the others are.
problems.solution: Each of the $[[k]]$ digits has $[[m]]$ choices, so there are $[[m]]^{[[k]]} = [[m^k]]$ codes.

problems.prompt: How many three-digit numbers use only the digits $0, 1, \ldots, [[m]]$? Digits may repeat.

mistakes.why: The first digit can't be $0$, so it has only $[[m]]$ choices.

hints: The first digit can be $1$ to $[[m]]$. The other two can be $0$ to $[[m]]$.
problems.solution: $[[m]]$ choices for the first digit and $[[m + 1]]$ for each of the others: $[[m]] \times [[m + 1]] \times [[m + 1]] = [[m*(m + 1)^2]]$.

problems.prompt: A menu has $[[a]]$ starters, $[[b]]$ mains and $[[c]]$ desserts. A meal is one main together with either one starter or one dessert (not both). How many meals are there?

mistakes.why: That would be a starter AND a dessert. Here it is a starter OR a dessert: add those first.

hints: The second course can be chosen in $[[a]] + [[c]]$ ways.
problems.solution: The extra course is a starter or a dessert: $[[a]] + [[c]] = [[a + c]]$ ways. With the main: $[[b]] \times [[a + c]] = [[b*(a + c)]]$.

problems.prompt: How many $[[k]]$-digit numbers have no two neighbouring digits the same?

mistakes.why: The first digit can't be $0$: it has $9$ choices.

hints: The first digit has $9$ choices ($1$ to $9$).
Each later digit can be anything except the digit just before it.
problems.solution: The first digit has $9$ choices, and each of the other $[[k - 1]]$ digits has $9$ (any digit but the one before). So $9^{[[k]]} = [[9^k]]$.

title: Multiplication principle challenge
instructions: Five AMC-style problems with choices (A) to (E), easiest first. You can leave a problem blank. Your answers are marked when you hand in the set, and you'll see a worked solution for each problem.

problems.prompt: A diner offers $4$ soups, $5$ sandwiches and $3$ drinks. A lunch is one soup, one sandwich and one drink. How many different lunches are there?

why.A: That adds the choices. One of each means multiply.

problems.prompt: How many four-digit numbers have all four digits even?
problems.solution: The first digit is $2, 4, 6$ or $8$ ($4$ choices); each other digit is $0, 2, 4, 6$ or $8$ ($5$ choices). $4 \times 5^3 = 500$, choice (C).

problems.prompt: Four squares in a row are each coloured red, green or blue. Squares that share a side must be different colours. How many colourings are there?

why.E: That ignores the rule that neighbours differ.

problems.solution: The first square has $3$ choices and each later square $2$ (not its left neighbour's colour): $3 \times 2^3 = 24$, choice (C).

problems.prompt: A palindrome reads the same forwards and backwards, like $12321$. How many five-digit palindromes are there?
problems.solution: The first three digits decide the number: $9 \times 10 \times 10 = 900$, choice (C).

problems.prompt: How many even three-digit numbers have all three digits different?
problems.solution: Last digit $0$: the first digit has $9$ choices and the middle $8$, so $72$. Last digit $2, 4, 6$ or $8$: the first digit has $8$ choices (not $0$, not the last), the middle $8$, so $4 \times 64 = 256$. Total $72 + 256 = 328$, choice (B).

title: Permutations
instructions: Type each answer and press Check. Order matters here; divide when items repeat. Stuck? Open a hint.

problems.prompt: In how many orders can $[[n]]$ people stand in a line?

mistakes.why: A person can't stand in two places: each spot has one fewer choice than the last.

hints: The first spot has $[[n]]$ choices, the next $[[n - 1]]$, and so on.

problems.prompt: $[[n]]$ runners finish a race with no ties. In how many ways can the gold, silver and bronze medals be given out?

mistakes.why: Order matters here: gold, silver and bronze are different prizes.

hints: Gold has $[[n]]$ choices. How many are left for silver?

problems.prompt: In how many ways can $[[a]]$ identical red flags and $[[b]]$ identical blue flags be hung in a row?

mistakes.why: The red flags look the same, and so do the blue ones. Divide by the ways to shuffle each colour.

hints: If every flag were different there would be $[[a + b]]!$ orders.
Divide by $[[a]]!$ and by $[[b]]!$.

problems.prompt: In how many ways can $[[n]]$ people sit around a round table, if turning everyone the same number of seats gives the same seating?

mistakes.why: Each seating was counted $[[n]]$ times, once for each turn. Divide by $[[n]]$.

hints: Seat one person anywhere. Then arrange the rest in a line going round.
problems.solution: Fix one person's seat; the other $[[n - 1]]$ can be arranged in $[[n - 1]]! = [[fact(n - 1)]]$ ways.

problems.prompt: $[[n]]$ people stand in a line, and two friends insist on standing next to each other. In how many orders can they stand?

mistakes.why: The two friends can stand in either order inside their block: times $2$.

hints: Glue the two friends into one block: now there are $[[n - 1]]$ things to arrange.
problems.solution: The block and the other $[[n - 2]]$ people: $[[n - 1]]! = [[fact(n - 1)]]$ orders. The friends can swap: $2 \times [[fact(n - 1)]] = [[2*fact(n - 1)]]$.

title: Permutations challenge
instructions: Five AMC-style problems with choices (A) to (E), easiest first. You can leave a problem blank. Your answers are marked when you hand in the set, and you'll see a worked solution for each problem.

problems.prompt: In how many different orders can the letters of the word MATH be written?

why.E: Each letter is used exactly once.

problems.prompt: How many different arrangements are there of the letters of the word LETTER?

why.E: Swapping the two E's (or the two T's) gives the same word.

problems.prompt: In how many ways can $6$ people sit around a round table, if seatings that differ only by turning everyone are the same?

why.E: Turning everyone one seat gives the same seating: divide by $6$.

problems.prompt: Five different books go on a shelf. Two of them, a dictionary and an atlas, must NOT be next to each other. In how many orders can the books go?

why.B: That counts the orders where they ARE together.

problems.solution: All orders: $5! = 120$. Together: glue them, $2 \times 4! = 48$. Apart: $120 - 48 = 72$, choice (C).

problems.prompt: Four-letter strings are made from the letters of PROBLEM, using each letter at most once. How many of them start with a vowel?

why.E: That is every string; only those starting with O or E count.

problems.solution: The first letter is O or E ($2$ ways), then $6 \times 5 \times 4$ for the rest: $2 \times 120 = 240$, choice (B).

title: Combinations
instructions: Type each answer and press Check. No order: divide the ordered count by $k!$. Stuck? Open a hint.

problems.prompt: How many committees of $[[k]]$ people can be chosen from $[[n]]$ people?

mistakes.why: That counts the members in order. A committee has no order: divide by $[[k]]!$.

hints: In order there are $\frac{[[n]]!}{[[n - k]]!}$ ways. Each committee appears $[[k]]!$ times.

problems.prompt: $[[n]]$ people meet, and every two of them shake hands once. How many handshakes are there?

mistakes.why: That counts each handshake twice (once for each person). Divide by $2$.

hints: A handshake is a pair of people: choose $2$ of $[[n]]$.

problems.prompt: How many shortest paths go from $(0, 0)$ to $([[a]], [[b]])$, moving one unit right or one unit up at each step?

mistakes.why: Each path is a string of rights and ups. Choose where the rights go.

hints: Every path has $[[a + b]]$ moves, $[[a]]$ of them to the right.
problems.solution: Choose which $[[a]]$ of the $[[a + b]]$ moves go right: $\binom{[[a + b]]}{[[a]]} = [[binom(a + b, a)]]$.

problems.prompt: A group has $[[b]]$ boys and $[[g]]$ girls. How many ways are there to choose $2$ boys and $2$ girls?

mistakes.why: That allows any $4$ people. You need exactly $2$ boys AND $2$ girls: multiply.

hints: Choose the boys: $\binom{[[b]]}{2}$. Choose the girls: $\binom{[[g]]}{2}$.

problems.prompt: A team of $[[k]]$ is chosen from $[[n]]$ players, and the captain must be on the team. How many teams are possible?

mistakes.why: The captain is already in. Choose only the other places.

hints: Put the captain in. Then choose $[[k - 1]]$ more from the other $[[n - 1]]$.

title: Combinations challenge
instructions: Five AMC-style problems with choices (A) to (E), easiest first. You can leave a problem blank. Your answers are marked when you hand in the set, and you'll see a worked solution for each problem.

problems.prompt: A pizza shop has $6$ toppings. How many pizzas have exactly $2$ different toppings?

why.C: Ham and olives is the same pizza as olives and ham: divide by $2$.

problems.prompt: How many diagonals does an octagon (an $8$-sided polygon) have?

why.C: That counts every pair of corners, including the $8$ sides.

problems.solution: Pairs of corners: $\binom{8}{2} = 28$. Take away the $8$ sides: $20$, choice (B).

problems.prompt: How many shortest grid paths (one unit right or up at a time) go from $(0, 0)$ to $(5, 3)$ and pass through $(2, 2)$?

why.A: Each first half can be followed by each second half: multiply.
why.D: That is all paths, not only those through $(2, 2)$.

problems.prompt: A panel of $4$ is chosen from $5$ teachers and $4$ students. It must have exactly $2$ teachers and $2$ students. How many panels are possible?

why.D: That is every panel of $4$, with any mix.

problems.prompt: Five points lie on one line and four other points lie on a second line parallel to it. How many triangles have all three corners among these nine points?

why.D: Three points on the same line don't make a triangle.

problems.solution: All triples: $\binom{9}{3} = 84$. Take away triples on one line: $\binom{5}{3} + \binom{4}{3} = 14$. $84 - 14 = 70$, choice (B).

title: Casework
instructions: Type each answer and press Check. Split into cases that don't overlap, count each, then add. Stuck? Open a hint.

problems.prompt: How many two-digit numbers have digits that add up to $[[s]]$?

mistakes.why: A two-digit number can't start with $0$, so $0[[s]]$ doesn't count.

hints: Split by the first digit: it can be $1$, $2$, … up to $[[s]]$.
problems.solution: The first digit is $1$ to $[[s]]$ and the second digit is then fixed, so there are $[[s]]$ numbers.

problems.prompt: How many three-digit numbers have middle digit $[[m]]$ and a middle digit larger than both of the other two digits?

mistakes.why: The first digit can't be $0$: it has $[[m - 1]]$ choices, not $[[m]]$.

hints: The first digit is $1$ to $[[m - 1]]$; the last digit is $0$ to $[[m - 1]]$.
problems.solution: First digit: $1$ to $[[m - 1]]$ ($[[m - 1]]$ choices). Last digit: $0$ to $[[m - 1]]$ ($[[m]]$ choices). So $[[m - 1]] \times [[m]] = [[m*(m - 1)]]$.

problems.prompt: How many pairs of positive integers $a < b$ have $a + b = [[n]]$?

mistakes.why: That counts $(a, b)$ and $(b, a)$ both. Here $a < b$, so count each pair once.

hints: Split by $a$: $a = 1, 2, 3, \ldots$ while $a < b$, that is while $a < \frac{[[n]]}{2}$.
problems.solution: $a$ can be any positive integer less than $\frac{[[n]]}{2}$, which gives $[[floor((n - 1)/2)]]$ pairs.

problems.prompt: How many triangles have whole-number side lengths and perimeter $[[p]]$? (Triangles with the same three side lengths count once.)
hints: Call the sides $a \leq b \leq c$. The longest side must be less than $\frac{[[p]]}{2}$.
Split by the longest side $c$ and count the pairs $a \leq b \leq c$ with $a + b > c$.
problems.solution: List the cases by the longest side $c$ (from about a third of $[[p]]$ up to just under half) and count $a \leq b \leq c$ with $a + b = [[p]] - c$. There are $[[floor((p*p + 24)/48)]]$ triangles.

problems.prompt: How many squares of any size are there on a $[[n]] \times [[n]]$ chessboard-style grid of unit squares?

mistakes.why: That counts only the small squares. Count the $2 \times 2$, $3 \times 3$ … squares too.

hints: Split by size. A $k \times k$ square fits in $([[n]] - k + 1)^2$ places.

title: Casework challenge
instructions: Five AMC-style problems with choices (A) to (E), easiest first. You can leave a problem blank. Your answers are marked when you hand in the set, and you'll see a worked solution for each problem.

problems.prompt: How many two-digit numbers have digits that add up to $7$?
How many triangles with whole-number side lengths have perimeter $15$? (Triangles with the same three side lengths count once.)
How many squares of any size are there on a $5 \times 5$ grid of unit squares?
How many three-digit numbers have digits that strictly increase from left to right, like $147$?

why.E: Each set of three digits can be written in increasing order in only one way.

problems.solution: $0$ can't be used (it would have to come first). Any $3$ of the digits $1$ to $9$ give exactly one such number: $\binom{9}{3} = 84$, choice (B).

problems.prompt: How many ordered pairs $(a, b)$ of positive integers have $ab \leq 10$?
problems.solution: Split by $a$: for each $a$ there are $\lfloor \frac{10}{a} \rfloor$ choices of $b$. $10 + 5 + 3 + 2 + 2 + 1 + 1 + 1 + 1 + 1 = 27$, choice (C).

title: Complementary counting
instructions: Type each answer and press Check. Count what you don't want, then subtract from the total. Stuck? Open a hint.

problems.prompt: How many $[[k]]$-digit numbers have at least one digit $0$?

mistakes.why: That counts the numbers with NO zero. Subtract it from the total.

hints: There are $[[9*10^(k - 1)]]$ numbers with $[[k]]$ digits.
With no $0$ at all, every digit has $9$ choices.

problems.prompt: A committee of $[[k]]$ is chosen from $[[b]]$ boys and $[[g]]$ girls. How many committees have at least one girl?

mistakes.why: That is every committee. Subtract the ones with no girls.

hints: All committees: $\binom{[[b + g]]}{[[k]]}$. All-boy committees: $\binom{[[b]]}{[[k]]}$.
problems.solution: $\binom{[[b + g]]}{[[k]]} - \binom{[[b]]}{[[k]]} = [[binom(b + g, k)]] - [[binom(b, k)]] = [[binom(b + g, k) - binom(b, k)]]$.

problems.prompt: $[[n]]$ different coins are flipped. In how many of the possible outcomes is there at least one head?

mistakes.why: That is every outcome. Take away the one outcome with no heads at all.

hints: There are $2^{[[n]]}$ outcomes. How many have no heads?
problems.solution: All outcomes: $2^{[[n]]} = [[2^n]]$. Only one has no heads (all tails), so $[[2^n]] - 1 = [[2^n - 1]]$.

problems.prompt: $[[n]]$ people stand in a line. Two of them must NOT stand next to each other. In how many orders can they stand?

mistakes.why: That counts the orders where the two ARE together. Subtract it from the total.

hints: All orders: $[[n]]!$. Together: glue the two, $2 \times [[n - 1]]!$.

problems.prompt: $[[n]]$ different coins are flipped. In how many outcomes are there at least two heads?

mistakes.why: The opposite of "at least two" is "zero or one". Also take away the outcomes with exactly one head.

hints: Take away the outcomes with no heads ($1$) and with exactly one head ($[[n]]$).

title: Complementary counting challenge
instructions: Five AMC-style problems with choices (A) to (E), easiest first. You can leave a problem blank. Your answers are marked when you hand in the set, and you'll see a worked solution for each problem.

problems.prompt: Two ordinary dice, one red and one blue, are rolled. In how many of the $36$ outcomes does at least one die show a $6$?

why.E: That is the outcomes with NO six.

problems.prompt: How many three-digit numbers have at least one digit equal to $5$?

why.E: That is the numbers with NO $5$.

problems.prompt: A code is three letters, each one of A, B, C, D or E; letters may repeat. How many codes use some letter more than once?

why.A: That is the codes with all letters different.

problems.solution: All codes: $5^3 = 125$. All different: $5 \times 4 \times 3 = 60$. So $125 - 60 = 65$, choice (B).

problems.prompt: Six people sit in a row of six chairs. Two of them, Ana and Ben, must not sit next to each other. How many seatings are possible?

why.A: That is the seatings where they ARE together.

problems.prompt: A committee of $4$ is chosen from $6$ men and $5$ women. How many committees have at least one man and at least one woman?

why.E: Take away the all-man and the all-woman committees.
why.D: Also take away the all-woman committees.

title: Warm-up for the check
instructions: Five quick problems, one from each lesson. Type each answer and press Check. Hints are here, but not in the check.

problems.prompt: A lock code is $[[k]]$ digits long, and each digit is one of $1, 2, \ldots, [[m]]$. Digits may repeat. How many codes are possible?

mistakes.why: Each of the $[[k]]$ spots has $[[m]]$ choices: multiply $[[m]]$ by itself $[[k]]$ times, don't multiply $[[m]]$ by $[[k]]$.

hints: Each digit can be chosen in $[[m]]$ ways, whatever the others are.
problems.solution: Each of the $[[k]]$ digits has $[[m]]$ choices, so there are $[[m]]^{[[k]]} = [[m^k]]$ codes.

problems.prompt: $[[n]]$ runners finish a race with no ties. In how many ways can the gold, silver and bronze medals be given out?

mistakes.why: Order matters here: gold, silver and bronze are different prizes.

hints: Gold has $[[n]]$ choices. How many are left for silver?

problems.prompt: $[[n]]$ people meet, and every two of them shake hands once. How many handshakes are there?

mistakes.why: That counts each handshake twice (once for each person). Divide by $2$.

hints: A handshake is a pair of people: choose $2$ of $[[n]]$.

problems.prompt: How many three-digit numbers have middle digit $[[m]]$ and a middle digit larger than both of the other two digits?

mistakes.why: The first digit can't be $0$: it has $[[m - 1]]$ choices, not $[[m]]$.

hints: The first digit is $1$ to $[[m - 1]]$; the last digit is $0$ to $[[m - 1]]$.
problems.solution: First digit: $1$ to $[[m - 1]]$ ($[[m - 1]]$ choices). Last digit: $0$ to $[[m - 1]]$ ($[[m]]$ choices). So $[[m - 1]] \times [[m]] = [[m*(m - 1)]]$.

problems.prompt: $[[n]]$ different coins are flipped. In how many of the possible outcomes is there at least one head?

mistakes.why: That is every outcome. Take away the one outcome with no heads at all.

hints: There are $2^{[[n]]}$ outcomes. How many have no heads?
problems.solution: All outcomes: $2^{[[n]]} = [[2^n]]$. Only one has no heads (all tails), so $[[2^n]] - 1 = [[2^n - 1]]$.

title: ⭐ Unit 9 check
instructions: Eight AMC-style problems with choices (A) to (E), easiest first, no hints. You need all 8 right to pass. Each try gives you different problems.

problems.prompt: A café has $5$ cakes and $4$ drinks. An order is one cake and one drink. How many orders are possible?

why.A: A cake AND a drink: multiply.

problems.prompt: How many three-letter strings of capital letters A to Z start with a vowel (A, E, I, O, U) and use no letter twice?

why.E: The first letter must be a vowel.

problems.prompt: How many four-digit numbers are odd and have all four digits different?

why.B: The first digit can't be $0$ either.

problems.solution: Last digit: $5$ odd choices. First digit: not $0$ and not the last digit, $8$ choices. Then $8$ and $7$ for the middle digits. $5 \times 8 \times 8 \times 7 = 2240$, choice (A).

problems.prompt: How many different arrangements are there of the letters of NOON?

why.E: Swapping the two O's (or the two N's) gives the same arrangement.

problems.prompt: $[[n]]$ runners finish a race with no ties. In how many ways can the gold, silver and bronze medals be given out?

why.A: Order matters: gold, silver and bronze are different.
why.D: One runner can't win two medals.

problems.prompt: Seven people sit around a round table; seatings that differ only by turning everyone are the same. Two of them must sit next to each other. How many seatings are possible?

why.A: The two can swap seats with each other: times $2$.
why.D: Turning everyone round gives the same seating.

problems.solution: Glue the pair: $6$ units round a table, $(6 - 1)! = 120$. Times $2$ for the pair's order: $240$, choice (B).

problems.prompt: How many different arrangements are there of the letters of CANADA?

why.E: The three A's can swap without changing the word.

problems.prompt: In how many ways can you choose $3$ books from $8$ to take on holiday?

why.D: The order you pick them in doesn't matter.

problems.prompt: $[[n]]$ people meet and every two of them shake hands once. How many handshakes are there?
A pizza shop has $8$ toppings. How many pizzas have exactly $2$ or exactly $3$ different toppings?

why.E: Two OR three toppings: add the counts.

problems.prompt: How many rectangles of any size are there in a $4 \times 3$ grid of unit squares?
problems.solution: A rectangle is fixed by $2$ of the $5$ vertical lines and $2$ of the $4$ horizontal lines: $\binom{5}{2} \times \binom{4}{2} = 60$, choice (C).

problems.prompt: How many two-digit numbers have digits that add up to $10$?

why.C: The first digit runs from $1$ to $9$, and each gives exactly one number.

problems.prompt: How many triangles with whole-number side lengths have perimeter $13$? (Triangles with the same three side lengths count once.)
How many three-digit numbers have digits whose product is $12$?

why.B: Don't forget $2, 2, 3$: it gives $3$ more numbers.

problems.solution: The digits are $1, 2, 6$ ($6$ orders), $1, 3, 4$ ($6$ orders) or $2, 2, 3$ ($3$ orders): $15$, choice (C).

problems.prompt: Six different coins are flipped. In how many outcomes is there at least one tail?

why.E: Take away the one outcome that is all heads.

problems.prompt: How many shortest grid paths (one unit right or up at a time) go from $(0, 0)$ to $(4, 4)$ and do NOT pass through $(2, 2)$?

why.B: That is the paths that DO pass through $(2, 2)$.

problems.prompt: How many four-digit numbers have at least one digit that appears more than once?

why.B: That is the numbers with all digits different.

problems.solution: All four-digit numbers: $9000$. All different: $9 \times 9 \times 8 \times 7 = 4536$. So $9000 - 4536 = 4464$, choice (A).

problems.prompt: A committee of $4$ is chosen from $5$ boys and $6$ girls. How many committees have at least $2$ girls?

why.D: Also take away the committees with exactly one girl.

problems.solution: All: $\binom{11}{4} = 330$. No girls: $\binom{5}{4} = 5$. One girl: $6 \times \binom{5}{3} = 60$. $330 - 5 - 60 = 265$, choice (C).

problems.prompt: Four ordinary dice of different colours are rolled. In how many of the $1296$ outcomes do at least two dice show the same number?

why.A: That is the outcomes with all four numbers different.
